title: Evaporation causes cooling
keyIdea: Evaporation cools the remaining liquid because the fastest particles are the ones most likely to escape as vapour, so the average kinetic energy of the particles left behind falls and the temperature drops. That is evaporative cooling — distinct from the water-cycle story of where evaporated water goes next.
familyTip: Dampen the back of your hand, then blow gently across it. Ask why it feels cooler: the fastest water particles leave as vapour, so the skin left behind has a lower average particle energy.

visual.caption: Evaporative-cooling idea or mix-up? Drag each clue, or tap it then a box.

items: remaining liquid has lower average KE
sweat cools you as it evaporates
cooling means the water cycle finished
temperature falls when average KE falls

lab.caption: Flagship lab: see fast particles leave, watch remaining KE and temperature fall, feel wet-skin cooling, catch heat/water-cycle mix-ups, then challenge.

kid: In a liquid, particles move at different speeds. The fastest ones are most likely to leave the surface and become vapour. That leaving is evaporation.
When the fast particles leave, the ones left behind have a lower average kinetic energy. Temperature measures that average, so the liquid cools. This is evaporative cooling.
Sweat cools you the same way: water on your skin evaporates and takes energetic particles with it, so your skin feels cooler. Wind helps by carrying vapour away.
This is not the same as the water-cycle story about clouds and rain. Here the key idea is why the liquid left behind gets cooler.
adult: Ages 12 to 14. Fast particles leave a liquid as vapour. The liquid that stays has a lower average energy, so it cools. This is not the water cycle lesson and not the general temperature lab.

Words: evaporation, kinetic energy, average KE, temperature, evaporative cooling. Common mistakes: thinking evaporation heats the liquid; mixing this with clouds; thinking only boiling cools; forgetting wind helps by taking vapour away.
In the lab the learner lets fast particles leave, sees average energy and temperature fall, links wet skin to cooling, spots mix-ups, and practises the idea.

choices: the fastest particles escape, so average KE of those left falls
every particle suddenly stops
the liquid always freezes first
practice.hint: Which particles leave, and what happens to the average energy left behind?
practice.explain: Faster particles are more likely to evaporate. The remaining particles have lower average KE, so temperature falls.

practice.prompt: A wet patch loses {a} fast particles out of {b} in a simple model. Particles still in the liquid?
practice.hint: Subtract the ones that escaped from the starting count.
practice.explain: {b} − {a} = {=b-a} particles remain in the liquid in this count.

choices: evaporation always heats the liquid
fast particles escape as vapour
remaining liquid can cool
practice.hint: Spot the claim that gets the temperature change wrong.
practice.explain: Evaporation cools the remaining liquid; it does not heat it. Fast escape and cooling of what is left are the real ideas.

practice.prompt: Average KE drops by {a} units in a simple model and temperature is taken as equal to that average. New temperature reading if it started at {b}?
practice.hint: Temperature falls with average KE in this simple model.

choices: water evaporates from your skin, removing energetic particles
sweat paints heat onto the air by colour
sweat only works when it freezes
practice.hint: Link skin water to evaporative cooling.
practice.explain: Evaporating sweat carries away higher-energy particles, so skin temperature falls. Freezing is not required.

pool.prompt: Temperature of a liquid links most closely to…
choices: the average kinetic energy of its particles
only the colour of the liquid
only how many clouds form later
pool.hint: What does temperature measure in the particle model?
pool.explain: Temperature reflects average particle KE. Colour and later clouds are not the measure.

pool.prompt: Wind can speed cooling of wet skin because…
choices: it carries vapour away so more liquid can evaporate
it paints the skin a colder colour
it freezes the sweat instantly
pool.hint: Think about removing vapour so evaporation continues.
pool.explain: Moving air removes vapour, so more energetic particles can leave and cooling continues.

pool.prompt: Evaporative cooling vs the water cycle: this lesson’s key point is…
choices: why the liquid left behind gets cooler
how rain forms in clouds only
that evaporation never happens below boiling
pool.hint: Separate cooling of the leftover liquid from the cloud story.
pool.explain: Here we explain cooling of what remains. Clouds and rain are the water-cycle path, taught elsewhere.

pool.prompt: In a model, {a} particles escape and each had {b} energy units above the average. Energy removed with them?
pool.hint: Multiply escaped count by the extra energy each carried.
pool.explain: {a} × {b} = {=a*b} energy units leave with the vapour in this model.

pool.prompt: Which particles are most likely to evaporate from the surface?
choices: the fastest ones
only the slowest ones
only particles at absolute rest
pool.hint: Who can break free of the liquid most easily?
pool.explain: Higher KE particles are more likely to escape as vapour.

choices: fast particles leave → average KE falls → temperature falls
temperature rises because vapour forms
liquid must boil before any cooling
pool.hint: Escape first, then average KE, then temperature.
pool.explain: Evaporation of fast particles lowers average KE; temperature follows. Boiling is not required for evaporative cooling.

pool.prompt: Start average KE = {a}. After evaporation it is {a}-{b}. Drop in average KE?
pool.hint: Subtract the new average from the start, or read the fall size.

pool.prompt: A puddle can cool as it evaporates even on a warm day because…
choices: escaping fast particles still lower the average KE of what remains
warm air forbids evaporation
cooling only happens in a fridge
pool.hint: Warm surroundings do not cancel the particle-escape effect.
pool.explain: Even in warm air, the particles that leave are the faster ones, so the remaining liquid’s average KE can fall.

pool.prompt: Patch A loses {a} fast particles. Patch B loses {a}+{b}. How many more escaped from B?
pool.hint: Subtract A’s escape count from B’s escape count.
pool.explain: B lost ({a}+{b}) and A lost {a}, so B lost {b} more.
